utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated; good morning. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technicians. I hope that the interpreters are here. I can hear them. Good morning, court reporters, legal assistants; good morning, counsel for the Prosecution. I can see that Mr. Michael Keegan is not here today, but I think that the counsel for the Defence are all present. Good morning to the accused. We will resume our hearing of the Kvocka and others case, and I hope that we will finally begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We made a ruling yesterday, but as regards the written request, we have already taken measures and we still insist on oral submission of motions. Everything that can be dealt with orally, I think we should try and do our best to proceed in that way. Ms. Hollis, the witness is already here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness we are calling, Your Honour, is Emir Beganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters are telling me that they cannot hear you. Could you speak up a little bit? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The interpreters have heard you this time. Could you please read the solemn declaration that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness, for coming to the Tribunal. I have to apologise for the inconvenience that has been caused to you, but I hope that now we will really begin with your testimony. You will first answer questions that will be put to you by Ms. Hollis. Ms. Hollis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Emir Beganovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: 27 October 1955, and I was born in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you known by any nicknames?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I have two nicknames: Braco and Began.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim by ethnicity, and I'm also Muslim by faith.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992, were you married, and at that time did you have children?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was married and I had one son.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you perform any military service?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I performed my military service in the former JNA, in 1975 and 1976.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duties or what was your speciality in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I served with the force engineers. I was with the Sappers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, prior to 30 May 1992, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I had my own business. I had a florist shop with my wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have any other businesses at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness also mentioned that he had a restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you had a florist shop and you had a restaurant business as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had cafes, restaurants; I had two businesses of that kind. And the fourth business was my florist shop, the one that was run by my wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were these businesses located?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all located in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The centre of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the centre of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time that you lived in Prijedor, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Until 1990 I lived in the area of Stari Grad, where I was born, and in 1990 I moved to the Esada Midzica Street, where I built a flat on the top floor of one of my catering businesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This area that you moved to in 1990, what area of Prijedor was that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The area in question was the centre of the town. It was the Esada Midzica Street, which ran parallel to the Marsala Tita Street. Behind the old Balkan Hotel, that's where the Esada Midzica Street was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, prior to the events that happened to you, beginning in May of 1992, how would you describe your family's financial situation?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a rather successful businessman. From a very young age, I was involved in business together with my father, and I was one of the wealthier men in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would have been the value of your assets as of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: According to my estimate, the damages that were caused to me during the war would be somewhere between 1.5 and 2 million German marks, if I take into account all the property that I had, all the businesses and the real estate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would like to offer a map of the town of Prijedor as an exhibit, and it would be Exhibit 3/76. We have provided copies of this map to Defence counsel yesterday, and we have additional copies for Your Honours and for the Registry. And if I could ask that that be put on the overhead. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, if you could take --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could the ELMO be pulled closer to the witness, please, so the witness may use it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, if you could take a moment to orient yourself on the map, please. Now, you mentioned that for a period of time up until 1990 you had lived in an area you called Stari Grad. Could you point to that area, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the area in question [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It appears to be an area that is surrounded by a canal or river; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the Sana River and this is a canal which is called Berek [indicates]. This is a kind of island which is called Stari Grad [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, on the map that you have, Mr. Beganovic, which is dated 1996, looking at the area you call Stari Grad, it appears that there are approximately two buildings in that area. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, prior to --

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a summer garden and a catering facility that was called Lovac. The rest was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, as of 30 May of 1992, approximately how many buildings were there in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think between 150 or 180, maybe 200 houses. Between 150 and 200.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of this area of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent Muslim. There was only one Serb who used to live in the area of Stari Grad. He didn't own any property; he lived there as a tenant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who did own property in that area?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Everything was privately owned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: By what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: All Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that there were houses there. Were there also businesses located in that area?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1990, some business facilities were built in one part of the park.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you know, what happened to all those buildings that used to be in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, they were plundered and then set on fire, and then bulldozers came and flattened the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that you lived and had businesses in the area you called the central area of Prijedor. Could you please show the Court what area you are talking about that your home and your businesses were located.

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: They were located in the centre of the town, in this area here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you're pointing to an area that is just, as we're looking at the map, to the right of the Stari Grad area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic composition of that area of the town?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: In that area of the town, the composition, the ethnic composition was mixed. All ethnic groups lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say "all ethnic groups", what ethnic groups are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. But there were others as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecutor offers into evidence Exhibit 3/76. And if the bailiff could retrieve that from the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any objections by the Defence? No? Very well, then. The exhibit is admitted, Ms. Hollis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, you have indicated that there were a variety of ethnic groups that lived in the Prijedor area. Do you recall when the elections were held in Yugoslavia, in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe they were held in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And within opstina Prijedor, what party won the majority?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that party was comprised predominantly of what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what other ethnic groups -- what other parties were there in the area at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: There was the SDA party, the SDS, the HDZ [Realtime transcript omitted "HDZ"], and the reformists that were led by Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of the SDS party, what was the predominant ethnic group, if any, of that party?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: They were almost 100 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I don't see it on the screen, but I believe you indicated the HDZ party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was the predominant ethnic group of that party?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned the reformist party. What was that party?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a party that was led by Ante Markovic. He was the founder of the party and he was in favour of improvement of economic situation, economic policy in the country, and he had quite a few followers in Prijedor. I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was that reformist party affiliated with any of these other parties?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How politically active were you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't politically active at all, except that Dr. Esad Sadikovic, Redo Marijanovic and myself, in 1991, at the end of the summer, we established the so-called League for Peace. The idea was to establish a kind of balance between the various parties. We were advocating peace. We wanted to attract people from all ethnic groups. We wanted to show people that a war was not necessary in Prijedor. We wanted to avoid the war. We were fighting for peace. That was the only option that was of any interest to us. But at the beginning of 1992, the league stopped functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the kind of activities that the league participated in to try to show people that war -- that war was not necessary in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, we organised this League for Peace, and at that time the majority of the members of the league were people from the town area, and they were full ethnic communities, Muslims, Serbs, Croats. We decided to organise public concerts. They were held in the town and the message we wanted to convey was the message of peace. We always managed to gather between 7.000, 8.000, sometimes even 10.000 people who would attend those concerts. So people were in favour of peace. However, the political parties did not like our activity, and very soon we did not have any opportunities to work and we had to stop functioning. At the end of March, or was it the beginning of April, I don't remember, we stopped functioning. We could no longer obtain permissions to organise concerts; we couldn't have any location for that. So our activities simply stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You say at the end of March or the beginning of April. Of what year?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you stopped because you could no longer obtain permission to organise. Who was denying you this permission to organise?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly the SDS party because the SDS party attempted to forcibly take power in Prijedor. We, from the League for Peace, managed to gather a large number of people. They went to the municipal building, to the town hall, and we had peaceful demonstrations and we managed somehow to postpone it for one month, for example. But the SDS was gaining more power and they were quite strong in Prijedor, so we no longer had any opportunity to act. And this is how the activities of the League for Peace stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that this League for Peace was created to show people that there was no need for war in Prijedor. Had you observed increasing tensions between ethnic groups in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the tensions began to mount after the breakout of the conflict in Croatia. The army, the JNA, was predominantly Serb, and they went to Croatia to fight there. But the Muslims rejected the callup to go to Croatia, and when they would come back from the front, from Croatia, they would walk around the town, armed. There would be shooting incidents. Weapons were being sold, including, for example, hand grenades. And this is what caused the tensions to mount at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated when "they" would come back from Croatia and "they" would walk around the town armed. What individuals are you talking about? What group?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Serb soldiers who went to Croatia to fight in Croatian cities, at the fronts in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to these Serb soldiers who had weapons, did you yourself observe other individuals in Prijedor being provided with weapons?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I didn't observe that. I didn't notice that anyone else possessed any weapons, except for the Serb soldiers who went to war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that weapons were being sold. To whom were these weapons being sold, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The weapons were being sold to everybody, to all citizens. Whoever had any money could obtain, could buy, weapons. An automatic rifle would cost up to 2.000 German marks, for example, and hand grenades were at the beginning between 20 and 30 German marks, and at the end they would sell for 10 German marks, for example. All those weapons belonged to the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In the Prijedor area during this time, when these tensions were developing, you indicated that you saw Serb soldiers walking around with weapons; there were incidents where weapons were fired. Did you observe any other military troops, equipment, or weaponry being moved into the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This took place every day. They would go to Croatia every day; they would come back from Croatia. People used to carry weapons around the town. Nobody tried to prevent that. There were lots of shooting incidents, lots of wounding incidents. It was common knowledge amongst the citizens of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, during the time period between February and the end of April of 1992, did you begin to notice any exodus of people leaving the town?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, people were leaving the town in great numbers. Every day buses would leave, and it was very difficult at that time to obtain tickets. Mostly Muslims and Croats were leaving the town; mostly women and children. People went to Croatia. Some of them stayed in Croatia and then later on they left for third countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did any members of your family leave Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my wife left the town with my son in mid-April. She went to Croatia, to the area of Istria. She was staying with her relatives in Labin. And she remained there until September, and in September she joined a convoy to the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, why did you have your family leave the town of Prijedor at this time?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Simply because it was already evident that the situation was unsafe, that something would happen. We had all expected some sort of fighting, but that the massacre would happen, no one could have imagined. All of us who sent our families away were fortunate because they escaped these terrible experiences.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: After you sent your family away, where did you reside?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The next day I moved to Dr. Esad Sadikovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned Dr. Sadikovic several times. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a doctor who had worked for the United Nations, but more recently he was in Prijedor. He was a specialist for nose, ear, and throat. He was one of the most prestigious citizens of Prijedor who lived before the war and during the war in the camp in order to help others. He was widely beloved by members of all ethnic groups. All of them respected him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Bosnian, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, why did you move to Dr. Sadikovic's house after your family left?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: He was related to my wife and one of my closest friends in Prijedor. We were best friends and we were very close, and I simply felt safer in his home than to go on living alone, even though tensions by then had already heightened. And I simply didn't feel safe living alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you fear would happen to you if you lived alone?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was afraid that at night someone might throw a hand grenade at me or open fire at me, which was a realistic prospect, because the Serbs who had armed themselves started mistreating citizens and taking revenge on them out of certain personal reasons. If simply they didn't like someone, they took their revenge on them. So people simply did not feel safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall, on the 29th and 30th of April, the Serb takeover of power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And after that event, what changes did you notice in the activities in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: They started out that same day. They hoisted their flags on all the important buildings in Prijedor, with the four S's on them. Then quite suddenly checkpoints cropped up in town at all major crossroads, in front of all important institutions, all over town, so that citizens had to pass through those checkpoints. They were mistreated, those who were Muslims or Croats. The Serbs could pass by without being stopped. So that the discomfort started the day they took over. The electricity was cut, though it was switched on and off occasionally. The media were taken over as well; the Serbs used them for their own ends. So that life changed overnight, within 24 hours. People moved around town less and less, so that after some 15 or 20 days, people stopped going out altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And did that apply to you as well? Did you stop going out?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did too. For the last ten days, I closed my establishments and I saw that there was no point in keeping them open. There were no customers; there was no business. The town was deserted. So I limited my movements to the street where Dr. Sadikovic's house was. We didn't need to go out of town anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was the last time that you were actually able to operate your businesses?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The end of April -- no. No, I'm sorry. The end of May, around the 20th of May, I think, was when I closed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prior to these tensions that had escalated in the Prijedor area, the clientele of your businesses were composed of what ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: They were of all ethnic groups. They would all come. However, as tensions escalated, the Serbs stopped frequenting Muslim establishments, not only mine but all Muslim cafes. They simply concentrated in those cafes owned by members of the Serb ethnic group. So that the divisions were evident in this area too, in terms of the catering institutions. It was known which were frequented by the Serbs, even though before the war we all used to go to the same cafes. But after this, there was some sort of a division.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'd like now to direct your attention to the events of the 30th of May of 1992. In the morning of the 30th of May of 1992, where were you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Dr. Esad Sadikovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And was there anyone else in his house with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A friend of ours, a common friend, a private caterer like me, Asif Kapetanovic, who was also known in town as a successful businessman, he was ill. He had kidney problems. And he was afraid to go to hospital, so that he spent the last two or three days at Dr. Sadikovic's house, who was giving him injections as treatment for his kidneys, whereas I had already been in that house for a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Asif Kapetanovic, what was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Bosnian of Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On the morning of the 30th of May, 1992, do you recall being awakened by Asif Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he woke me up. I was sleeping. The previous night we sat together, until late. I had a bit too much to drink, so I slept firmly. I didn't hear the shooting. When he woke me up, I heard the gunfire. I got up, got dressed, looked through the window and saw that troops were moving around, wearing various uniforms, police uniforms, camouflage uniforms, olive-grey uniforms. We switched on the radio and started listening to the programme, and announcements were made giving instructions to how the Muslims should behave; that they should stay home, that they should be at rest, that they shouldn't move around. And then later on they said that all Muslims should hang out white flags. Those who didn't have flags, white sheets, so that the Muslim houses could be identified by these white flags, which Esad and myself did. On both sides of the house, we hung up a white sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you for a moment, sir. When you looked out to the town, you indicated that you saw individuals in different kinds of uniforms moving around. Did you, when you looked out, see any signs of destruction to any areas of the town?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't see any destruction. But when we were hanging up these sheets, we climbed upstairs and I could see Stari Grad from Dr. Esad's house, and I saw that it was burning. All over Stari Grad houses were burning. I could roughly spot by parents' home, and I could see that there was a flame and smoke there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And were your parents still in Stari Grad at this time?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I thought my mother was in the house, but later on it turned out that she was lucky enough not to be in the house. She was staying with my sister in another part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Kapetanovic, did he observe any destruction to any buildings that he owned or that his family occupied?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After some time, maybe half an hour, Asif saw that his cafe bar was burning, and above that cafe was his family apartment. This was, from Sadikovic's house, as the crow flies, some 100 metres. And he saw that the flames were about 10 to 20 metres high. The whole house was on fire. And he screamed, "My mother's inside. She must be burning." I decided to go with him. We reached the house; however, the next-door neighbour told Asif that his mother had left the house prior to the fire and that she was alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, as you moved from Dr. Sadikovic's house so this area in the old town, what, if anything, did you hear as you moved toward that area?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes. As you moved from Dr. Sadikovic's house towards Asif Kapetanovic's shop, where his mother lived, what, if any, sounds did you hear in the streets?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The shooting was still going on, and a soldier came up, or he was some 30 or 50 metres away from us and he shouted "Stop". I turned around and saw that he was carrying a rather large rifle, something bigger than an automatic rifle. It could have been a machine-gun. So I said to Asif, "I'm not going to wait for him, I'm going to run." There was a hedge of the house, I jumped over it and I heard two or three short bursts of fire. I was lucky not to have been hit. I went into the yard. I knew it was a Muslim house. I knocked on the door and the door was opened and I went inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, how long did you remain at that house?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The family where I went inside were listening to the radio, and the instructions on the radio were that the Muslims should come out with white ribbons around their arms, that they should form a line and head towards the centre of town, towards the high-rises there. In Muharem Stojanovic's street, there were three high-rises, and they still exist, and we were instructed to congregate there. Some of the people stayed there and another group was taken towards the Balkan Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, as you and these people moved toward this area, were there any escorts that you had?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the time. There were members of the Serb police, the army, people in uniform, in camouflage military uniform, and there were others wearing blue police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what weapons, if any, did these individuals have?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: All of them had weapons, and they were mostly carrying automatic rifles, pistols, grenades attached to their belts, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As you moved toward this centre point that you had been directed toward, did you see any dead bodies as you went there?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As we were moving along the pavement, next to a small open market, on the pavement I saw a pile of some four or five bodies, one on top of the other, thrown into a pile. I glanced across the marketplace and I saw another two or three bodies beneath the fruit and vegetable stalls. They were all civilians. They had no military insignia on them or uniforms or weapons. There were no weapons there either. They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise any of these people?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I was not able to recognise them because they had probably been mutilated by machine-gun fire, so I couldn't recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you reached this centre point, how many people were at this central point?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: There were perhaps about 2.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these people?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew most of them. I saw my mother there, sister, my brother-in-law, and all the other citizens, most of whom I knew quite well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic group of these people that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were Muslims, but there were some Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened once you reached this central point?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing, really. We saw there were about ten buses from the city transport parked there. They gave us orders for the men over 15 years of age to go to one side, and children under 15 and women to go to the other side, which we naturally did. We had to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, once you were separated into groups of one group of men, one group of women and children, what was done with the group of men?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: We were loaded onto the buses, a column of buses was formed, and the buses set off towards the SUP building in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On your bus, how many people were on your bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a driver in uniform and one or two escorts. I think two escorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how many people who had been arrested were on your bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: About 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that one or two people, as escorts, were on your bus. What kind of uniforms did they have?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And did you recognise what kind of uniforms those were?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise either of those escorts?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: In my bus, no, I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that once you got on the buses, then you moved in the direction of the SUP. Were you given any instructions as to how to conduct yourselves on the bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: They said we should bend down our heads, not to look out the windows. The column of buses stopped in front of the SUP. We stayed there for five or ten minutes. They probably went inside to get instructions, and then they came back, these escorts, and the column started off again. We reached the JNA Street and then Partizan Street, and then we went directly to Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what is Tomasica?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a village outside Prijedor, about 20 kilometres from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And from Tomasica, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't reach Tomasica. Before we reached Tomasica, we took a left turn. And afterwards, I realised -- actually, I never used that road -- the road led to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What time of the day did you arrive at Omarska? Was it during the daytime? Was it at night?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: It was getting dark by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And at the time that your bus arrived at Omarska, how many other buses, if any, also arrived?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw our column of some ten buses arriving.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when your bus arrived, where did it stop?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: It stopped near the so-called pista, actually, next to the restaurant in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what happened after your bus stopped there?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they took some ten men at a time from the bus, searched them, took all their valuables from them, and told them to go into this room behind the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you say when you arrived there, "they took ten men at a time and searched them." These individuals who took the men off and searched them, were they waiting there for you when your bus arrived?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what type of clothing were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: They were also in blue police uniforms, in camouflage uniforms, in olive-grey uniforms. There were all kinds. They were all of Serb ethnicity, the army, the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of weapons, if any, did these individuals?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly automatic rifles and pistols and hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And these individuals that took you off the bus and searched you, did you later see any of these individuals while you were detained in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see most of them. I would see them all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And these individuals that you saw, what were their duties at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Some were leaders and others were ordinary guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you yourself were taken off the bus, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: They told me to take out everything from my pockets, and as I happened to be wearing a jean jacket, which I hadn't worn for a long time previously, I put my hand in a pocket and I took out a couple of crackers. And he saw me put them down on a bench and he said, "You can execute this one because he used these to try and confuse our army." So I was taken aside and I waited for them to take me to execute me. Then somebody started pushing me by the shoulders inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could stop there for a moment. You indicated that you took something from your pocket. What was it that you took from your pocket?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Ordinary crackers, fire crackers that people throw at New Year's, and I also had some papers in my pocket and they happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And then you indicated that, "He saw me put them down," meaning the fire crackers, and "he said you can execute this one." Who is the "he" you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He used to be a guard in the camp, Pavlovic or Palic. He had a dark complexion and dark hair and he had a lock of white hair. I think he spent all of his time in the camp as a guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During your detention at Omarska, did you come to associate him with one particular group of guards, one particular shift?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And which shift was that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say "Krkan's shift", that's how that shift was referred to in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that after this search and after you were taken aside, that eventually you were moved into a building. What building were you moved into?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken to a building behind the restaurant. The place was referred to as Mujo's room. The soldier pushed me in but I didn't know who he was. I didn't know where they were taking me. I thought I would be killed. But this guy was wearing a blue police uniform, and when I turned, I recognised him. He was an active professional policeman in Prijedor for a very long time. He told me to go there, and when I entered the room, I saw approximately 600 to 700 people. Most of them were known to me. And he told me, "Just go there and hide. Don't answer when they call you. If you answer, you will be killed. If your name is called out, just don't answer. Just pretend you're not there. This is how much I can help you, and this is all I can do for you. Just go there and hide somewhere." And he turned around and left after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you willing to tell the Court the name of this man who gave you those instructions?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't do it now. I know him very well by sight. He used to be on duty very often in the centre of the town, in the street where I had my cafes and my restaurant. And I would see him very often but I can't remember his name at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that when you went into this room you referred to as Mujo's room, that you thought there were perhaps some 600 people in that room. Did you recognise any of those people?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew most of them. My cousin was there, for example. There were lots of people who were my neighbours from the Stari Grad area. Lots of men from Stari Grad were there. There were also people from the area called Lukavica, and I knew all of those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And your cousin who was there. What is your cousin's name?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Mirsad Beganovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, these people that you knew in this room, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were Muslims, but there were some Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, how long did you remain in Mujo's room after you were taken in there that night, that evening?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I only spent that night there. The place was crowded; I think there were over 1.000 people there. We could hardly breathe, and there was of course no room for us to lie down. And in the following morning, half of the people were taken to the pista and one half remained in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And were you taken to the pista or did you remain in the room?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, how long were you held on the pista?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I remained there between 10 and 12 days, on the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And from the pista, where were you held?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken from the pista to the "white house" first, where I was badly beaten up. And two days later I was transferred to the room referred to as "Petniska" which means room number 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that room 15 was in what building?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: In the building called "hangar".

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how long were you held in that room?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed one month, perhaps a little less than that, in that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And then from room 15, where were you next held?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I was taken for interrogation on the upper floor of the restaurant building where offices were, offices that were used for the interrogation of detainees. And after that I was taken back to the pista, and on the same day I was transferred to Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This is the same Mujo's room you referred to earlier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, was there any other location at the Omarska camp that you were held prior to you being taken from the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a small garage there which was not bigger than 20 square metres, I think. I spent two nights and two days there. There were perhaps 160, 170 of us there, I don't remember, but the situation was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when was it that you were actually taken from Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to have the witness move to the model and point to the various locations he has described for you. To do that most effectively, I believe we will need the assistance of the technical people to operate this camera. Is it possible to have that assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Hollis, the witness may approach the model, and we'll did our best, as I see that Mr. Dubuisson is in contact with the technical booth.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the bailiff could assist the witness with the microphone and the headset, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that Mr. Tosic wishes to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, for interrupting. There were quite a few leading questions by the counsel for the Prosecution as regards a number of certain dates. For example, the 30th of April, the 30th of May. There were also a few questions if the witness had seen any corpses, instead of asking him, for example, what was it that he saw. There were a number of leading questions. I should like Your Honours to have that in mind. As regards the statement of the witness, there are some discrepancies and that's why I believe that it was a leading question. The witness should have been asked a question like where he was on the 30th of April and the event itself should not have been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that Mr. Fila also wishes to intervene, so perhaps you can respond after that. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to state for the record that the witness, while approaching the model, cursed the accused, Mladjo Radic. Everybody could hear that. We all heard him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't curse him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we could all hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, can you respond to the objection raised by Mr. Tosic?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution submits that there are instances where, in order to focus the testimony and save time, you can indeed lead the witness. You can refer them to a certain date. If the Defence is saying that there is a dispute about when the takeover of Prijedor occurred, that is one of the facts that they have agreed to. So my submission is that these were attempts to focus the witness, to expedite the relevant testimony. These are supposedly not facts that were in dispute. And the issue about whether he saw dead bodies, he could say yes or no, and then he went on to describe them. We suggest that these were not unduly leading questions. They were attempts to focus and direct the testimony to relevant parts. If we were to ask him what happened on that day, we'd sit here for two hours and hear him describe everything. It was an attempt to focus the testimony. Regarding discrepancies in testimony and prior statements, alleged discrepancies, that's a matter for cross-examination. So we believe that the questioning was appropriate. It was not unduly leading and that the discrepancies are a matter to be addressed in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that Ms. Hollis is right. We will also be mindful of the remark raised by the Defence. It is true that we did not reach a ruling on judicial notice yesterday, but we said that we take notice of a number of facts which are agreed upon by both parties. We are going to apply normal rules in this particular testimony, but we are not forgetting that there is an agreement and one has to bear that in mind. Otherwise, we will never finish this case. You always have the right to intervene, but it has to be a justified intervention. We have to bear in mind that we agree that certain dates are correct, are agreed upon, and that is why I think we can proceed in a speedy fashion. And it is not necessary to incorporate everything in the examination-in-chief, but I didn't want to interrupt. We are trying here to have a good procedure, to make it better. I thank you for your remark, for your intervention. You always have the right to intervene, but you should do it only if it is absolutely necessary to do so and if it is useful. You may continue. As regards the conduct of the witness, I did not notice that, and the witness should bear that in mind, as he knows what he has said or done. But I didn't hear anything. We have to be very careful about that in the future. Ms. Hollis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have referred to the bus arriving at Omarska and stopping by the building you referred to as the restaurant building. Would you please point to that building?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: It was here [indicates]. This is the restaurant and this is the entrance to the restaurant [indicates]. This is the restaurant building [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the entire building, is there a term by which that building is referred to?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Here [indicates]?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The building you were just pointing to.

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The restaurant building. That's how we referred to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned an area called the pista. Could you point out that area, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the area here [indicates], located between the restaurant and the hangar, the whole of this area here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the hangar. You're referring to the long building across from the restaurant as the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this building here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned a building you called the "white house". Could you point to that building?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the building in question [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We don't see anything on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't respond to that, Your Honour, because I don't know the technical. I'm told that it was on the video. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you see it now, Your Honour? Could they focus on the camp again with the camera, please? I think perhaps, Your Honours, we're having technical difficulties, but we will move along with this. If the bailiff could please remove the roof of the building called the restaurant building, the restaurant building here. If you could move the roof that's toward the back of the building. Yes. And we are now looking at the first floor of the building with the roof off.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, could you please point to the room where you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in this room here [indicates] B9.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And B9 is the number that appears in that room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The number that you just read, is that the number that appears in that room?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, this is the room in question, B9 [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if the first floor of that building could be taken off, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could point to the room you have referred to as Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: This room here [indicates], A9.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that is the number that appears in that room on the model; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if the other roofs could be taken off that building, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned the restaurant part of that building. Could you point to that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Here [indicates], A22.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, during your time at Omarska, did you become familiar with a room that was referred to as the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I would pass by that room when we went to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were never in that room?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you point to where this room called the "glass house" is on the model?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the room marked A14 [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you've also referred to being in the "white house", being beaten there and also being held there. Could you move to the "white house" and could you show us first the room or rooms you were in in the "white house" when you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the building in question [indicates]. I was in room A6, the second room on the right side, looking from the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So as you enter the building, the second room on the right is the room to which you're referring; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also indicated that you were held in the "white house" for a short time. Could you point to the room or rooms in which you were held?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I was held one night in room A3, the first room on the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you held in any other rooms in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I also spent one night in the toilet, A5.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And where is that room located as you enter the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: It was straight ahead from the entrance, A5. That was the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have also mentioned being held in a room you called "room 15" in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the bailiff could take the roof off the front part of the hangar, the part facing the "white house", the long part facing the "white house", if that could be taken off.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if the witness could please point to the room you referred to as "room 15".

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the room [indicates], B7, and it led to room B8 and B23. You could access those two rooms from that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And as you went into the -- as you went into the hangar building, did you -- where was that room in relation to the stairs?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: On the right side. We would enter here [indicates], then we would climb up the stairs, and on the right side was the door leading to that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If the witness could please resume his seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, would this be a convenient time for a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we think that this witness and several other witnesses which will follow is a very important witness for us. We should like to have an effective use of this break, and we would like to contact our client here in the vicinity of the courtroom. We should kindly ask for our client not to be led downstairs, and I think that this will assist us in our work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dubuisson, as regards the logistics, are any difficulties in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will see about it, Your Honour. I will see if there are any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. If it is possible that this contact is allowed, and when we come back, if there are any problems -- I should like the witness to leave the courtroom before us, in order to avoid any conflict. So the witness will only be brought in after the Judges have entered the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry I had to take this measure, but it is in order to avoid any problems, any conflicts. We will have a 20-minute break now. The break will be a 30-minute break so that the requested contact can be made. A 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the witness enters, the Prosecution feels it necessary to put on the record that my colleague was observing the witness as he moved to the model and did not observe any indication of his lips moving to say something, nor hear any derogatory comments. In light of the Defence assertion, we wanted to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. Hollis. You may continue. But still, there is tension that one can feel in the courtroom and we have to contain it. So please continue, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Beganovic, you indicated that you spent the first night in this room called Mujo's room and that the next day you were taken to this pista area that you have identified for the Court. Now, this next day when you were taken to the pista area, did you see any uniformed personnel in this area?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw soldiers in military uniform, policemen in blue uniforms. They were moving around. There was a vehicle next to the pista, a police car, a police armoured vehicle, which had its barrels turned towards us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this police armoured vehicle with its barrels pointed toward you, did you come to associate that vehicle with a certain group of people?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One could see that the Serb army controlled that vehicle and that they were holding us in their sights in case of any rebellion or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, the people that you saw and associated with this vehicle, were these people that you saw throughout your detention in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I saw them for the first 10 or 12 days, and through contacts and stories, we could come to the conclusion that they came from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, these individuals that you saw for the first 10 to 12 days in Omarska, what was their conduct toward detainees? What did you observe of their conduct toward detainees?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they treated us roughly. They wouldn't let us go to the toilet; they wouldn't give us water; they wouldn't give us food. For the first six days I didn't get a single piece of bread. It was on the sixth day that I got some food.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This abuse that you talk about, what time of the day or night did this abuse occur?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: This would happen during the day and during the night. Every minute, every second, they wouldn't leave us alone. There was always someone who was being physically mistreated. Psychologically, of course, they were taking people up there for some sort of interrogation, to the premises above the restaurant. People would come back; in 99 per cent of the cases, they were beaten up. This started straight away, the very first days.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this group that you believed came from Banja Luka, what, if anything, did you observe of the interaction between this group and the regular camp personnel?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They contacted amongst themselves, as if they all belonged to the same military unit, or the police administration. They behaved in the same way, the people from Banja Luka, as well as those from Prijedor municipality. They cooperated; they collaborated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this unit you believed to be from Banja Luka, when they were in the camp and they were engaging in this abuse of detainees, did you ever observe anyone intervene to stop this abuse?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No one prevented them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever observe anything that appeared to you to indicate they were punished for this abuse?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. No one was ever punished, nor could we get the impression that they were being contained in these efforts. On the contrary. They were being praised when they physically mistreated the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, the camp personnel, other than this unit you believed to be from Banja Luka, did you know any of these camp personnel as people that you had been acquainted with or seen before the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew a couple of those who were permanently in the camp. I knew Kvocka; I knew Koka, the man known as Koka, who came to the camp on a daily basis. He used to sell chicken and that's why he got the came Koka, which means a chicken. I knew him for many years. Then I know some others who would come to the camp occasionally, but they were not guards in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, the ones that came to the camp on a daily basis, you mentioned Kvocka and Koka, and you said that Koka was a man you had known for some time previously. When you saw him in the camp, what did you see him doing in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Koka?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Koka.

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Koka kept lists; he was constantly compiling lists. He would come to the room known as number 15. Down there in front of the hangar, he would line us up and make these lists. For what purpose, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During what period of time in the camp did you see Koka in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I would see him while I was in number 15, so that would mean mid-June until the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw him, what kind of clothing did he wear?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Koka, I think, wore a blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of weapons, if any, did you see him have?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you knew him prior to the camp. What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you knew Kvocka. Who was Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Kvocka was a policeman, and I knew him as an employee of the SUP. I knew that for a while he was in Omarska and in Prijedor. I knew his wife. His wife lives some 100 metres from my house. She's roughly the same generation as I. I knew his brothers-in-law, with whom I grew up. I knew that he was their son-in-law. My mother was friendly with his mother-in-law. She would go and visit his apartment, and his mother-in-law -- one year they went to the seaside together, my mother, Kvocka, his wife, and his mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you knew Kvocka's wife. What was her father's last name?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, during what period of time did you see Kvocka in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I would see him in the camp immediately as soon as I came, the first few days, and then later -- then I didn't see him while I was in number 15, but when I left number 15, I saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you were on the pista, how often would you see Kvocka in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I would see him non-stop, every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And during what periods of the day or night did you see him?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I would see him during the day, not at night. He would enter, as far as I can remember, in a 190 Mercedes car. He would usually come to this corner of the restaurant [indicates]. Then he would bring cigarettes, food, drinks, and he would distribute it to the guards more or less every day, and he carried --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt for a moment. You pointed to an area of the restaurant. So that it's clear on the record, what part of the building were you pointing toward? The restaurant side that you identified or --

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The side where the restaurant is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when you indicated he would come to this area in a car, are you talking about him coming to the area that is closest to the hangar or the area that is farthest away from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: It would be the area on the corner of the restaurant, that's where the car would usually be parked, and he would take out things from the boot of the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you're talking about the corner of the restaurant, looking at the restaurant area, are you talking about the corner of the building that is closest to the hangar or the corner that is farthest away?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The way you are looking at it, the right-hand corner of the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So the corner that is farthest away from the hangar.

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, further away from the hangar, the area towards the "white house".

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to seeing Kvocka doing these things, what else did you observe him do?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: He was quite conspicuous. He wore gloves with the fingers cut off. He carried a pump-action gun all the time, known as Pumperica. And he would walk around all the time, issue orders to them of some sort. Simply he was their boss and they obeyed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to walking around in the camp, when, if ever, did you observe him go into any buildings of the camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: He would enter through the main entrance very often. Then he would go upstairs to the offices or downstairs. I don't know. He would go in and out quite often, whenever he was in the camp. He was constantly on the move.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when you say that he would enter through the main entrance and go into this building, what building are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: The building of the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever observe him go into any other buildings?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't really interested at the time. He moved around everywhere, all over the camp. He was walking around all the time. He was on the move, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, while you were in the camp, Kvocka actually provided you, or made it possible for you to have a package; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that package was from whom?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a package from my mother, who took the parcel to his mother-in-law. He personally didn't deliver it but the package reached me. True, all that my mother had sent was not inside, but something was inside, some underclothes and some food. This was towards the end of July or the middle of July, around there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to this one occasion where Kvocka made it possible for you to have a package, were there any other occasions when he made it possible for you to have a package?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I personally received a package that once. As far as I know, my mother told me that she sent -- she carried packages a couple of times. But I received one only once.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to these two individuals you have named as individuals you knew prior to coming to the camp, during your detention in Omarska, did you come to know and recognise any other camp personnel?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In due course we learned more or less all the names of the guards, Paspalj, Krkan, Krle. Then there was someone known as Joja. He had his gun pointed at us above the restaurant when we were lying on the pista. Soskan, Pirvan, and others. During our detention, we came to learn their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the person referred to as Krkan, is that a proper name or a nickname?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how did you come to know and recognise that person with the nickname Krkan?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Simply all the detainees knew it. Everyone knew who was Krkan and who was Paspalj. They addressed each other by name like that, so there was no difficulty in learning who was who.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how often would you see Krkan in the camp while you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: While I was at the pista, I would see him while he was on duty. Then while I was in number 15, I couldn't -- I was immobile, so I didn't go out and I couldn't see them. Then when I moved from 15 to Mujo's room, occasionally when we would go out into the fresh air, they would let us out occasionally, so he would come by, I would see him. But I saw him most often during the first 10- or 12-day period.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when you saw him, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. He was walking around there. Sometimes he would stand over there, where the round circular glass is, at the entrance [indicates]. He would just pass by there. I didn't have any particular contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And you say that sometimes he would stand where the circular glass is. What building are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The building of the restaurant, the entrance to the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw Krkan, what weapons, if any, did he have?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I think he carried an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated some other names as well. For example, Paspalj. How did you come to know him?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: He would come into Mujo's room frequently and physically mistreat the detainees. He would select at random. He was drunk all the time and he would come in and shoot inside, he would beat people, he and Soskan, and the others. They were there where the kombi is, the entrance near Mujo's room, there used to be a kombi van, and they used to eat and drink there. And then when they felt like it, they would enter our room and mistreat us, abuse us, physically, psychologically.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when this mistreatment occurred by Paspalj and the person you referred to as Soskan, when, if ever, did camp personnel intervene in this mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No one ever intervened. They could do what they wanted. Nobody cautioned them or reprimanded them or punished them. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned a person by the name of Krle. Would that be a proper name or a nickname?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: A nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how often would you see this person in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EMIR BEGANOVIC
utterances.text: I would see him too during the first period. While I was in number 15, I didn't see him. And then when I left number 15 and went to Mujo's room again, during the last days of my detention, I was taken out, I think, three times in the evening. I was blackmailed; they wanted money from me. And he would stand next to the entrance with this Brk, who was in the camp. He would come in a green Mercedes. I think he was a taxi driver in Omarska before the war. And I was blackmailed. They wanted 100.000 German marks from me to be transported by helicopter to Belgrade, or 50.000 for Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Witness, for interrupting you. Excuse me, Ms. Hollis, but I think Mr. Nikolic wishes to intervene. Do you have any objection, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just referring to what you said as the president, that we should object if there is a good reason. I think that the Defence counsel of the accused Kos has good reason to do this now. I would like the Prosecutor to limit herself to the examination as regarding the circumstances that Witness Beganovic would be asked about as indicated. I think that the Prosecutor has expanded beyond what was stated in the submission, beyond the scope of what was stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the objection, Your Honour. I asked a question that, the Prosecution submits, was relevant. The witness has answered the question, and we submit that the information being provided is relevant. I'm not aware that there is a limitation on the scope of questioning in direct, other than relevance, compared so some limitation that may exist on cross-examination. So I must confess I'm not quite clear of what the nature of the objection is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, can you explain better what is the grounds for your objection? The questions are beyond the scope of the indictment or what? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm holding the Prosecution's submission of the 23rd of February this year, compiled in accordance with Rule 65(C), and the Prosecutor has given an attachment and the first witness is Emir Beganovic on that list. In accordance with Rule 65 ter (iv), under (C), the Prosecutor has indicated which points in the indictment each witness will be testifying about. That is how the Defence understands it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Nikolic, do you feel that the question goes beyond the indictment? It is the indictment that is important here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This particular question to the witness is beyond the scope of the indictment. That is the position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, do you understand the objection now?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. And the Prosecution's position is that it is not beyond the scope of the indictment. The indictment talks about conditions in the camp; it talks about abuse of all the prisoners in the camp. This relates to that matter. It relates to a person who has been identified as a personnel within the camp. It is being related to you by a witness who was in the camp and observed it, and now is the subject of about what he is about to discuss with you. Also, Your Honours, part of the indictment is that money was taken from people. He's talking about a blackmail situation here. We believe that this evidence is relevant to and within the scope of this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
